Mia did not spend long studying the surface. She went straight at anything loose, especially square of the wicket, and those early boundaries did more than lift the score; they forced Windshore to spread before they had settled into their own bowling plan. Aria Bennett, at the other end, was quieter at first, not passive, just measured, letting Mia take the sharper edge of the opening phase while she got a read on pace and bounce. That opening burst mattered because it meant Riverstone were never stuck in a slow start, even though the first wicket came through fielding rather than bowling. Sana Malik’s run out of Mia gave Windshore a visible breakthrough, and at that moment there was still a chance for the innings to compress. Riverstone had lost the batter who had supplied the immediate spark. The reason the innings did not flatten was Aria. She absorbed that wicket almost without changing the emotional rhythm of the match. Nora Fields came in and gave her the exact kind of partner a set captain needs: calm enough not to chase everything, busy enough not to let the innings drift, and clean enough through the off side to punish the over that strayed. The second-wicket stand became the real spine of the innings. It did not feel like one long explosion. It felt more controlled than that, almost repetitive in the way it kept putting Windshore back under the same pressure. A tidy ball would be followed by a worked single. A defensive field would be followed by Aria finding the gap anyway. Nora did not overhit, but she kept giving the partnership shape, and every time Windshore looked as if they might drag the run rate down, one boundary or one loose wide would undo the pressure they had just built. Leena Farooq was the one bowler who gave Windshore genuine control for a stretch, hitting a fuller line and making the batters earn more of their movement, but too much of the rest of the attack leaked. Sana Malik was involved in the field, but her overs were expensive. Riya Shah and Zara Khan both had moments where the ball was there to be hit. Noor Ali’s single over at the back end disappeared quickly enough to make the closing overs feel even heavier. By the time Nora finally fell, caught off Leena, the stand had already reshaped the match. Riverstone were no longer building toward a useful score; they were threatening a score that could make the chase feel oversized before it had even started. Lena Hart came and went quickly after finding one clean hit, but that wicket did not restore the innings to Windshore because Ivy Quinn arrived with the correct closing mood. She did not need a long look. The field was out, the bowlers were under fatigue, and Aria was still there, which meant Ivy’s job was simply to make the final overs sharper. She did that neatly, finding the rope, running hard, and allowing Aria to finish from the center rather than forcing the captain into desperate late hitting. Aria’s innings was the complete hand of the match: fast enough when it needed to be, patient enough through the middle, and still present when the last over closed. Riverstone’s total therefore had layers. Mia gave the launch, Aria gave the control, Nora gave the long support act, and Ivy added the finishing punch. Windshore did not bowl terribly from every end, but they never found enough wickets to interrupt the innings properly. Two wickets by the final phase would not be enough against a set captain playing that cleanly, and the extras they conceded made a strong card look even fuller. Chasing one hundred and eighty-two was always going to ask for more than one good partnership, and Windshore’s problem was that they never found the second and third layers Riverstone had found. Sana Malik and Riya Shah began cautiously, almost too cautiously for the size of the chase, but at least they survived the first spell long enough to avoid an immediate collapse. Clara Bell eventually removed Sana, and that wicket increased the required pressure without yet ending the pursuit. The only real window for Windshore came when Lara Noor joined Riya. Lara was not explosive, but she gave Riya someone stable enough to bat around, and for a few overs the chase had a pulse. Riya was the one batter who looked capable of making Riverstone work deeper into the innings. She found the rope, took advantage when the line became too straight, and kept enough scoring movement alive that Windshore could still tell themselves the game had not fully gone. Then the key break came, and it was not just a wicket in the scorebook. Lara’s run out by Pippa Lane cut the one partnership that had made the chase feel structured. After that, Riverstone tightened almost instantly. Mira Stone removed Riya soon after, and once the set batter had gone, the reply lost the only player who had made the target feel even faintly negotiable. Leena Farooq tried to keep the middle together, but Ava Reed had her caught behind before she could turn occupation into recovery. Zara Khan was pinned by Mira, Asha Mir was bowled by Ivy Quinn, and each dismissal made the chase less like a pursuit and more like a side trying to avoid being bowled out. Noor Ali was taken out by Nora Fields, Hina Qureshi could not survive Ava’s return, and even though Saira Joseph stayed to the end, she was doing survival work in a match already far beyond reach. Meena Patel’s late boundary added a tiny flash, then the final-ball run out underlined the pressure Riverstone had kept applying even after the result was obvious. That is the important distinction in this reconstructed match: Windshore were not blown away in one chaotic over. They were denied continuity. They had an opening pair that survived without scoring quickly enough, one useful stand that gave the innings a brief middle, and then a steady sequence of removals that left no route back. Riverstone defended the total in stages. Clara Bell opened the door, Pippa Lane’s fielding broke the only settled pair, Mira Stone removed the batter who mattered most, and Ava Reed made sure the lower middle could not rebuild. Aria Bennett’s Player of the Match award fits because her unbeaten innings was the difference between a strong Riverstone total and a total that felt overwhelming. Yet the win was not just one batter carrying a side. Riverstone’s batting innings had proper architecture, and their bowling innings had proper timing. Windshore, by contrast, had individual flashes but no complete phase after the second-wicket stand was broken. By the final over, the margin felt natural rather than inflated: Riverstone had made a layered high score, then defended it with enough discipline to prevent Windshore from ever turning survival into pressure.

Grace Linden’s unbeaten eighty-six was a major innings in its own right and would have been the headline in many other matches, but here it sat beside a captain’s all-round performance that shaped almost every decisive phase. By the end, Bayview Royals Women had played a match almost entirely on their own terms: huge opening control, clean late batting, early bowling incision, middle-order suffocation, and a ruthless finish. Sandbank Spirits Women were beaten first by the size of the target, then by the speed with which their chase lost structure, and finally by a bowling unit that refused to let even a huge cushion soften its standards.
